title: Two more Fed hikes, then a long pause: Goldman reads a third hot core CPI print
body: A January hike is a step beyond what the market has firmly priced, so Goldman's call leans against any rally at the front end. The two-year yield's jump to near 4.86% shows how quickly expectations can move. For the dollar, a longer tightening cycle supports the policy divergence already weighing on currencies such as the yen and the Aussie. Gold is vulnerable too, since it has repeatedly fallen as Fed hike expectations rise rather than acting as a haven. Equities face the same pressure on valuations seen across AI names this month. The key test is whether Fed officials start to talk openly about January before the December meeting. --- The latest jaw boning from the Fed: Hammack: Economy can handle more restriction, unclear how far Fed has to go --- Three strong core inflation readings in a row have convinced Goldman that summer's slowdown was a blip. It now expects the Fed to hike in January as well as December before taking a long breather. Summary: Goldman Sachs Asset Management expects the Fed to hike in December and again in January, followed by a prolonged pause. US core CPI rose 0.3% in October, an annualized pace of about 3.6%, beating expectations for a third firm reading in a row. The summer's softer prints now look temporary rather than the start of a disinflationary trend. Strength was broad, spanning supercore services, housing and core goods, which makes it harder for the Fed to look through the data.

title: Japan delays its first 2-year floating-rate JGB: what it says about BOJ bets
body: The delay has little direct effect on JGB supply, since the floater never launched and the issuance plan is still being drafted. Its value is as a signal. The issuer itself is saying that investors see little need to hedge against BOJ tightening, which suggests front-end yields already price in a hiking path. That makes the market more sensitive to any upside surprise from the BOJ: if policy tightens faster than priced, short-dated JGBs would reprice and the case for floaters would quickly return. For the yen, the read is neutral to mildly supportive, since it confirms that rate expectations are already high. The November 26 meeting with primary dealers is the next place to watch for hints on how the fiscal 2027 plan will reshape issuance across maturities. Newswire cut: Japan is postponing a new two-year floating-rate government bond as markets already price in BOJ hikes, sources told Reuters, reducing the appeal of a product built to shield investors from rising yields. No new launch date has been set for now. One-line wrap: Tokyo built a bond to protect investors from BOJ rate hikes, but the bond market has already priced the hikes in. So the insurance has gone back on the shelf before it was ever sold. Summary: Japan's Ministry of Finance is postponing a planned two-year floating-rate government bond, according to two sources. Issuance had been targeted for as early as January, and no new date has been set while the ministry reassesses demand.

For FX, gold's slide adds to the headwinds facing the Australian dollar, which is already near its weakest levels since January. --- Gold has given up more than 30% from January's record as rising yields and a strong dollar outweigh its inflation-hedge appeal. title: RBA minutes: 6 members saw rates "not clearly sufficient", 3 warned of sharper downturn
body: On balance the minutes lean hawkish, unsurpisngly. The majority's view that 4.85% is "not clearly sufficient" sits awkwardly with market pricing that had all but ruled out further hikes, and it backs up Bullock's comment this morning about upside risks. The minority's warning of a sharper downturn sets a high bar for a December move, though. This week's wage and jobs data, and the October CPI jump the staff flagged in advance, matter more than usual. For the Australian dollar, near 0.6730, the minutes are mildly supportive but unlikely to change the trend while policy diverges from the Fed. The minutes treat oil as the swing factor: if prices hold rather than ease by around US$30 a barrel as assumed, the inflation case for another hike strengthens. --- Earlier RBA's Bullock says inflation risks still skewed to upside ahead of 6-3 vote minutes --- The RBA majority hiked because 4.85% might not be enough, and the minority held back because the economy might already be cracking. That leaves the next move hostage to this week's jobs data and the oil price. Summary: Six of nine RBA board members backed November's hike to 4.85%, judging the cash rate "not clearly sufficient" to address upside inflation risks. The majority cited strong market services inflation, high unit labour costs, broad cost pressures and a likely rise in the neutral rate.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6715 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

Any further disruption in Europe or the US during the Thanksgiving peak would bring airline and travel stocks into focus. The banking outages were resolved and described as technical. They're more a reminder of operational risk than a credit or stability concern. --- Also: Iran drawing up dirty bomb options for Washington, 7 US officials say, not seen imminent --- Washington is warning Americans to watch their step in Europe this holiday season. Back home, a week of grounded flights and frozen bank apps has shown that the systems people rely on can fail without any attacker involved. Summary: The US Embassy in Bulgaria issued a Europe-wide security alert urging Americans to stay vigilant during the holiday season. It warns that terrorists, including lone actors, could target markets, transport hubs, malls and places of worship with little warning. Strikes and demonstrations have become more frequent, and hoax bomb threats disrupted flights in numerous European countries in November. Americans are advised to monitor local news, check with airlines, avoid demonstrations and enroll in the State Department's STEP alert program.

title: China resumes crude stockpiling, leaving room for fuel exports at 3 times prewar margins
body: For crude, China's return to stockpiling adds a source of demand alongside refinery consumption. That supports import levels even while runs are soft, and helps cushion prices against weaker demand elsewhere. The bigger lever is in products. With refineries running below 80% and diesel margins near triple their prewar level, more export quotas from Beijing could send significant volumes of fuel into Asian markets and narrow those margins. For now the signal points the other way: diesel exports are falling and November tracking is weaker. The tightness in middle distillates looks set to persist unless policy changes. --- China has come through the Hormuz shock with its oil reserves intact and is rebuilding again. It also has plenty of idle refining capacity, so whether diesel margins stay this high depends largely on Beijing's export quotas. Summary: China added close to 490,000 bpd of crude to its stockpiles in October, reversing a draw of around 530,000 bpd in September. Crude imports rose to about 9.9 million bpd, the highest since March, while refinery runs slipped to around 13.7 million bpd. Over the first 10 months of 2026, China has still added about 270,000 bpd to its inventories despite the disruption from the Iran war. Fuel exports fell to about 5.2 million tons in October, and diesel exports dropped to around 310,000 bpd from a near three-year high in September. Refineries are running at less than 80% of capacity, so there's scope to increase exports.

title: RBA's Bullock says inflation risks still skewed to upside ahead of 6-3 vote minutes
body: Bullock's comment pushes back modestly against market pricing that has all but ruled out a December hike. It could offer the Australian dollar some support after it fell this week to its lowest level since late January. One line on a panel is unlikely to shift pricing on its own, so the minutes are the bigger test. Any sign that the majority on the board saw a real chance of further tightening would firm up the hawkish reading of Bullock's remarks. If the minutes play up how close the vote was, front-end rates may decide the governor's comment is a hedge, not a signal. - Minutes preview here: Economic and event calendar in Asia Tuesday, November 17, 2026: RBA minutes, plus Bullock - Bullock says inflation risks are still tilted higher. That reminds markets that a split board doesn't mean the RBA is done, just as the minutes are due to show how close the debate was. Summary: RBA Governor Michele Bullock says inflation risks remain skewed to the upside. She made the remarks at a panel in Sydney, shortly before the release of the November meeting minutes. The RBA raised its cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth hike this year and the highest level since 2008, in a 6-3 vote. Markets have priced out nearly all chance of a December rate rise. The minutes are expected to show how the board weighed inflation risks against a slowing economy. Wage data on Wednesday and October jobs figures on Thursday round out the week.

The more market-relevant point is the regional source's warning that hardliners who benefit from the war could try to wreck talks over the coming weeks. That keeps the outlook for a deal to reopen the strait fragile. A US homeland incident is a low-probability event with severe consequences. It would probably hit risk assets broadly, and more as a shock to risk appetite than as a direct supply story for crude. --- US officials say Iran has drawn up specific options for a dirty bomb or chemical attack on Washington. Summary: New US intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans that could target senior administration officials in Washington with a dirty bomb or chemical weapon. Officials see the planning as Iran building options, not as a sign of an imminent attack, although the intelligence reportedly includes specific locations and targets. title: Iran says 4th tanker hit in 24 hours as UKMTO reports Hormuz attack near Oman
body: For oil, an attack in the narrowest part of the Strait of Hormuz hits the main export route for Gulf crude directly. That supports the risk premium even before any supply loss is confirmed. Crude has recently held back from reacting to unverified Iranian claims, so independent confirmation of multiple strikes is the trigger to watch for a sharper move. Higher war-risk insurance premiums and owners rerouting or delaying transits would tighten effective supply even if no cargo is lost. The US force-protection build-up suggests Washington is not expecting a quick de-escalation. --- An attack in the narrowest part of Hormuz has left a tanker disabled and on fire. Iran says it has now hit four in a day, and the US is pouring concrete for a long stay. Summary: A tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was disabled by an attack about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, at 1900 GMT on Monday. The attack caused an engine room fire. The crew are reported safe, and damage and environmental impact are not yet known. Iran's navy says it has hit four oil tankers in the past 24 hours. The link to this incident is not confirmed. Tehran claimed over the weekend that a supertanker sank after hitting a mine, which remains unverified. The US Army is seeking 17 concrete bunkers for bases in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Lebanon within 45 days, citing risks to troops from Iranian fire. A third US carrier strike group has arrived in the region.

title: Intel slides 7% as investors sue over PC slump disclosures, extends losses after hours
body: A lawsuit rarely changes a company's fundamentals, but this one keeps attention on Intel's weakest point, the PC business, at a time when the stock has already lost about half its value in six months. The supply argument cuts both ways. Shortages of substrates and memory limit how fast Intel can capture data center demand, and they also weigh on PC makers. That ties into the industry-wide memory squeeze flagged by Goldman Sachs. Nvidia's results are the next big test of chip sentiment. Any sign that supply constraints are loosening across the sector would matter more to Intel's shares than the legal case. --- Earlier: Goldman Sachs: chip stocks near 3-year valuation low even as demand outruns supply --- Investors are suing Intel. They allege its upbeat AI talk masked a worsening PC slump and supply shortages, and the lawsuit reopens the wound from October's record one-day plunge. Summary: Intel shares closed about 7% lower on Monday near $55.50 and fell around 3% further after hours. A proposed class action filed on Friday alleges Intel misled investors about the hit from slowing PC sales and excess inventory. The complaint also alleges Intel concealed that supply limits prevented it from meeting data center demand. The suit covers investors who bought shares between July 23 and October 29. October's results sparked a one-day fall of nearly 29%, wiping out around $140 billion of market value.

title: Goldman Sachs: chip stocks near 3-year valuation low even as demand outruns supply
body: If Goldman is right that the market is already pricing in an earnings slowdown that hasn't arrived, beaten-down chip names could recover quickly on any upbeat earnings or guidance. Nvidia's results are an obvious near-term test. The memory squeeze matters well beyond the US. It feeds directly into Asian chip heavyweights such as Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC, and so into the Kospi and Taiwan's benchmark. The stress on selectivity points to dispersion rather than a sector-wide rebound. Memory, equipment and supply-chain names look better placed than the most crowded GPU trades. --- Chip stocks are priced as if an earnings downturn is coming, but Goldman sees demand running ahead of supply and multi-year visibility. It argues the sell-off has created buying opportunities for investors who choose carefully. Summary: Semiconductor stocks have sold off sharply in recent weeks even as fundamentals have strengthened. Demand is running ahead of supply in memory, server CPUs and chipmaking equipment. Memory makers are signing multi-year supply deals, and equipment suppliers are planning for higher spending into 2027 and 2028. Demand is broadening beyond GPUs into high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, networking and power. Tight memory supply is now hitting PCs and consumer devices too. Nvidia's leadership transition is seen as more likely to shift market share gradually than to disrupt the AI investment cycle. The sector trades at about 13x forward earnings.
